title: Linked List Cycle
statement:
Decide whether following `next` references from the head of a singly linked list ever revisits a node.

Contract
- `head` may be null or may point to the first node of a list. Each node has an integer `value` and a mutable `next` reference.
- A list has a cycle when some node can be reached again by following `next` references. A node may link to itself.
- Return true when the list has a cycle and false when the walk reaches null.
- Node values may repeat, so equal values never prove a cycle; only the same node object does.
- Do not modify the list and do not record visited nodes in a collection.

Examples
- A list `1 -> 2 -> 3` that ends in null has no cycle.
- A list `3 -> 2 -> 0 -> -4` whose last node links back to the node holding `2` has a cycle.
- A single node whose `next` is itself has a cycle.

examples.input: head = 3 -> 2 -> 0 -> -4, tail links back to index 1

hints: Walking forward forever will not terminate on a cycle, so you need two walkers moving at different speeds.
Advance one walker one step and the other two steps per round; if the fast one reaches null there is no cycle.
If the walkers ever stand on the same node, the list has a cycle. Intended complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space, where n is the number of nodes before the walk repeats or ends.
inputSyntax: Input: the list values followed by the index the tail links back to (-1 for none), for example: [3, 2, 0, -4] 1
